cards.title: Speed is how fast, velocity is how fast where
cards.body: Speed is distance over time: 100 meters in 10 seconds is 10 m/s. Velocity is speed with a direction attached: 10 m/s north. Two cars can share a speed but have opposite velocities, and physics treats them as completely different motions.

cards.title: Acceleration is the real main character
cards.body: Acceleration is change in velocity over time. Speeding up, slowing down, and turning all count, because turning changes direction. A car cruising at steady 60 km/h in a straight line has zero acceleration; the moment it turns, it is accelerating.

Units are the cheat code. Meters per second (m/s) for speed, meters per second squared (m/s²) for acceleration. If your answer's units are wrong, the number is wrong — checking units catches most mistakes before they happen.

A cyclist covers 300 meters in 25 seconds.
Speed = distance ÷ time = 300 ÷ 25 = 12 m/s.

That's about 43 km/h — fast for a bike, which is exactly why the number is worth a second look. Sanity-checking answers against the real world is a physics superpower.

cards.q: A car drives 60 km/h north, then 60 km/h south. What changed?
cards.explain: Speed stayed 60 km/h, but direction flipped, so velocity changed. Velocity always includes direction.

flashcards.back: Slowing down, or turning at constant speed — both change velocity.

questions.q: A runner covers 200 m in 40 s. What is the speed?

choices: A car turning a corner at steady speed
A car parked at a light
A car cruising straight at constant speed
questions.explain: Turning changes direction, and direction is part of velocity. Changing velocity is acceleration.

choices: Because motion in opposite directions is physically different
questions.explain: 60 km/h north vs 60 km/h south are different motions with different effects, like momentum.

questions.q: A ball's velocity changes from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s. Acceleration?
questions.explain: (20 − 0) ÷ 4 = 5 m/s². Change in velocity over time.

questions.q: Your answer comes out in m/s but the question asked for acceleration. What's wrong?
questions.explain: Acceleration is velocity change over time, so its units are m/s². Wrong units mean a wrong setup.

cards.title: Objects are lazy: Newton's first law
cards.body: An object keeps doing what it's doing unless a force interferes. A puck slides across ice nearly forever because friction is tiny; it stops on carpet because friction is huge. This laziness has a name: inertia, and mass measures how much of it an object has.

cards.title: F = ma: the most famous equation in physics
cards.body: Force equals mass times acceleration. Push twice as hard, get twice the acceleration. Double the mass, halve the acceleration for the same push. And Newton's third law: every push gets pushed back — the rocket pushes exhaust down, the exhaust pushes the rocket up.

Draw the arrows. A free-body diagram is just the object with every force as an arrow: gravity down, the table pushing up, friction opposing motion. Once the arrows are on paper, F = ma turns into simple addition instead of a word puzzle.

You push a 2 kg box and it accelerates at 3 m/s².
F = m × a = 2 × 3 = 6 newtons.

Six newtons is about the weight of an apple in your hand — small forces move small masses impressively fast, which is why the numbers deserve a reality check.

cards.q: A rocket fires exhaust downward and rises. Which law is this?
cards.explain: Third law: every action has an equal, opposite reaction. Exhaust goes down, rocket goes up.

flashcards.front: State Newton's first law in one sentence.
flashcards.back: Objects keep their motion unless a net force acts on them.
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
An object's resistance to changes in motion; measured by mass.

questions.q: A 4 kg cart accelerates at 2 m/s². What force is pushing it?
Why does a hockey puck glide so far on ice?
choices: Friction is tiny, so almost no force stops it
questions.explain: First law: with barely any friction, the puck keeps its velocity.

questions.q: You push a wall and it pushes back. You don't move because:
choices: The forces balance — net force on you is zero
questions.explain: The wall's push cancels yours. No net force, no acceleration — that's the third law in action.

questions.q: Two boxes get the same push. The heavier one accelerates less because:
choices: Greater mass means more inertia (F = ma)
questions.explain: For the same force, acceleration = F/m. More mass, less acceleration.

questions.q: What is the net force on a book sitting still on a table?
choices: Zero — gravity and the table's push cancel
questions.explain: Gravity pulls down, the table pushes up equally. Balanced forces, zero net, zero acceleration.

cards.title: Moving things carry energy
cards.body: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: KE = ½mv². Notice the v² — doubling your speed quadruples the energy, which is why a 100 km/h crash is four times as violent as a 50 km/h one, not twice. Speed is expensive.

cards.title: Height is stored energy
cards.body: Lift something and you store gravitational potential energy: PE = mgh (mass × gravity × height). Drop it and the stored energy converts to motion. A roller coaster is just this trade running back and forth, which is why the first hill is always the tallest.

Energy never appears or vanishes, it only changes form. This conservation law solves problems that forces can't touch: a pendulum's speed at the bottom follows directly from the height it fell, no stopwatch needed. When stuck, ask: where did the energy go?

A 2 kg ball sits on a 5 m shelf. Take g = 10 m/s².
PE = m × g × h = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 joules.

Knock it off and all 100 J become motion (ignoring air). Conservation of energy just predicted the landing speed without tracking a single force.

cards.q: Why is a 100 km/h crash four times worse than 50 km/h?
cards.explain: KE = ½mv². Double the v, quadruple the energy.

What is the formula for gravitational potential energy?

flashcards.back: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only transformed.

questions.q: A 1 kg ball moves at 4 m/s. Its kinetic energy?
Where does a roller coaster move fastest?
choices: At the top of the first hill
questions.explain: Potential energy is lowest at the bottom, so kinetic energy — and speed — is highest there.

questions.q: You lift a box to a shelf. Where did your effort go?
questions.explain: Work becomes stored PE = mgh. Drop the box and it converts back to motion.

choices: How fast work gets done (work ÷ time)
questions.explain: Power = work/time, in watts. Energy is the amount; power is the rate.

questions.q: A pendulum swings but each swing is slightly lower. Why?
choices: Friction and air resistance steal energy as heat
questions.explain: Energy is conserved overall — some just leaks into heat and sound instead of motion.
